intro:
Khalkhin Gol — 20 August 1939

Comrade, the border fighting has become a battle between the Soviet-Mongolian grouping and the Japanese Kwantung Army. Both sides have reinforced, and Zhukov is ready to use his armour to turn the Japanese flanks.

Break the enemy line, take Nomonhan and its airfield, and clear the remaining marked strongpoint. Keep our forward positions and airbase secure while the mobile columns advance.

Japanese infantry can hold its ground stubbornly even when its tanks are outmatched. Pin the strongpoints with infantry and guns, then use armour to get beyond them. The aim is to cut off the enemy grouping, not batter every position from the front.

Now the Japanese have asked for an armistice, and they agree to abide by the existing border! Congratulations, you have been awarded the title of "Hero of the Soviet Union", promoted to General of the Army, and have been given command of the Kiev Special Military District!

intro:
Chisinau — 28 June 1940

Romania has accepted the Soviet ultimatum to evacuate Bessarabia and northern Bukovina. The withdrawal is under way, but the handover of roads, towns and railway equipment is confused, and armed forces are moving through the same narrow routes.

Your assignment in this scenario is to occupy Chisinau and Manoilesti while securing the approaches already held by our troops. Move quickly enough to control the junctions before retreating columns or local resistance can obstruct them.

This campaign turns the occupation into a tactical battle. It should not be read as a record of a full-scale Soviet-Romanian battle for the city. Keep your force together and concentrate on the marked objectives.

intro:
Yelnya — 30 August 1941

The Germans hold a salient around Yelnya, close enough to threaten another advance towards Moscow. Their infantry has dug into the villages and approaches, and the position has survived earlier Soviet attacks.

The Reserve Front is to squeeze out that salient. Take Yelnya, Sadki, Yaroslavl and Khanino while keeping Pozhogino and Kostyuki secure behind the attack. Removing the bulge will shorten our line and deny the Germans their forward base.

Use the artillery to break connected defensive positions rather than sending isolated units against them. Infantry must hold the shoulders of each penetration while the mobile troops move on the next village.

intro:
Istra — 6 December 1941

Comrade General, the German advance on Moscow has been stopped, but its forward troops still occupy the towns and roads north-west of the capital. The winter counteroffensive begins now, before those positions can be made permanent.

Drive the enemy out of Istra, Solnechnogorsk and the other marked settlements while keeping Moscow secure. Each junction recovered pushes the threat away from the capital and gives our own columns a road forward.

The enemy is exhausted, not helpless. German infantry and guns can turn a village into a costly obstacle. Keep the riflemen, armour and artillery within supporting distance and do not leave an open road back to Moscow.

intro:
Rzhev breakout — 29 November 1942

The attacks of Operation Mars have driven Soviet mobile formations into the German defences around Rzhev, but some of the forward troops are now cut off. The immediate problem is to reopen the connection before the pocket is crushed.

Attack the German-held objective at Bolshoye Kropotovo and protect our positions around Novoselovo and Gorskovo. The defenders hold the bottleneck; concentrate enough infantry and artillery to break it instead of scattering the force through the surrounding villages.

This map represents the breakout through objective capture. Securing the marked objectives determines the result; there is no six-unit evacuation requirement in this version. Keep the corridor covered once it is open.

Operation Iskra — 12 January 1943

Leningrad remains cut off by land. Between the city and the Volkhov Front lies a narrow German-held strip south of Lake Ladoga, fortified around settlements, woods and industrial sites.

The two Soviet fronts are attacking towards one another. Capture Shlisselburg, Lipka and the marked workers' settlements, and clear the other objectives including Nazija Airfield. Opening this corridor will restore a land connection to the city; it will not by itself end the entire siege.

The German Eighteenth Army has had time to prepare its positions. Use infantry and engineers with close artillery support, and secure the ground between the advancing groups so the new corridor cannot be cut again.

Operation Kutuzov — 15 July 1943

The German attack north of Kursk has stalled. Soviet forces have opened their counteroffensive against the Orel salient, and Rokossovsky's Central Front is joining the pressure from the south.

Advance beyond Ponyri, take Ponyri-Pervyje, Tagino and the other marked enemy positions, and keep our own Ponyri base secure. The local breakthrough supports the wider effort to force the Germans out of the salient before they can rebuild their line.

Expect prepared infantry positions covered by artillery and anti-tank guns. Clear the first belt deliberately, then exploit with the mobile troops. Do not let a success at one village leave the next column without support.

Kamenets-Podolsk — 21 March 1944

The First and Second Ukrainian Fronts are pressing into the German position in western Ukraine. Their advances threaten the roads by which the First Panzer Army can withdraw from the Kamenets-Podolsk area.

Take Dunayevtsy, Kamenets-Podolsk, Dracynci and Chernovtsy while protecting the Proskurov and Tsyhany approaches. The towns and crossings are the hinges of an encirclement: leave a route open and the German mobile formations may escape through it.

Your armoured columns must move quickly, but they cannot hold a wide ring alone. Bring infantry up to the junctions and keep a mobile reserve against a concentrated breakout.

Bagration: choose your front — 22 June 1944

The offensive against Army Group Centre is about to begin. Headquarters offers two assignments: support the First Belorussian Front on the southern approach, or join the Second Belorussian Front farther north.

Move to Staging Area 1 to take the First Belorussian route, beginning at Bobruisk. Move to Staging Area 2 to take the Second Belorussian route, beginning at Mogilev.

This is a campaign route-selection map. Choose the front you want to accompany before committing to its staging area; the next battle will give you that front's operational orders.

The German Ninth Army is defending the southern shoulder of the Belorussian front. Bobruisk has been designated a fortress, and the roads through it offer a route west for troops threatened by our breakthrough.

Break the defensive belt, take Bobruisk and the marked positions around Telusha, Bortniki and Gorodets, and keep Mormal Airfield secure. The purpose is both to seize the town and to open the southern route towards Minsk.

Use infantry and artillery to force the first gaps, then send the mobile troops towards the junctions. The German garrison must not be given time to turn a withdrawal into a new defensive line.

Brest-Litovsk — 18 July 1944

The collapse of the German front in Belorussia has opened the way west. The First Belorussian Front is extending its offensive on the southern flank, beyond the Pripet marshes.

Take Brest-Litovsk and the marked junctions through Kobryn, Pruzany and Scianka, together with the western objectives and Dzivin Airfield. Keep Bereza secure behind the advance. These roads carry the pursuit and offer the enemy routes out of the threatened area.

Retreating troops still have guns and armoured reserves. Keep the columns connected and clear the crossings before committing the heavy equipment. A swift pursuit needs a road that stays open behind it.

Praga — 10 September 1944

The Germans still hold Praga on the eastern bank of the Vistula, across the river from Warsaw. Their bridgehead threatens our line and blocks an approach to the capital, where the uprising continues.

Clear the marked eastern-bank positions, including Rembertow, Targowek and the two Praga sectors, while keeping Goraszka secure. This operation is for Praga and its approaches; taking them does not mean the whole of Warsaw has been liberated.

The defenders can use streets, railways and fortified buildings to break up an attack. Advance with infantry under artillery cover, and keep the tanks out of unsupported street fighting. Secure the river approaches as the line moves forward.

Mogilev — 23 June 1944

Comrade Marshal, the Second Belorussian Front is attacking the German Fourth Army. Mogilev controls roads towards Minsk, and the defenders must be held here while the neighbouring fronts break through farther north and south.

Capture Mogilev, Orsha and the other marked positions, including Tolochin Airfield, while keeping Gorki secure. Seizing the junctions will deny the Germans a convenient route for reserves and withdrawal.

Expect organised infantry resistance along the approaches and river lines. Bring the artillery and engineers forward before committing armour across a narrow crossing. The army needs a breach that the following formations can use.

Novogrudok — 5 July 1944

Minsk has fallen, and German formations east of the city are being cut off. The next task is to keep the retreat from settling into another front along the roads towards Grodno and Bialystok.

Take Novogrudok, Lida, Grodno, Volkovysk and the other marked junctions. Keep Minsk and Pinsk secure behind the advance. Neighbouring Soviet armies are continuing the offensive, but your own columns must hold the routes they open.

The distances now favour mobile troops; the towns still favour determined rearguards. Avoid leaving isolated detachments to guard a whole line of communications. Bring the rifle formations forward as each new junction falls.

Osowiec — 6 August 1944

The pursuit has brought the Second Belorussian Front to the approaches of the Osowiec fortress. Its crossings and nearby settlements stand across the next advance towards Lomza and East Prussia.

Take Osowiec and the marked objectives at Goniadz, Monki, Kulesze and Zucielec. Keep Suchowola secure while you push through the defensive belt. The fortress is valuable because it controls the route ahead, not merely because it is a prominent name on the map.

German infantry can make good use of the restricted approaches. Reconnoitre the crossings, bring up the guns and let engineers and riflemen open a passage for the armour.

Stargard — 1 March 1945

The German counterattack from the Arnswalde sector has been checked, but enemy forces in Pomerania still threaten the northern flank of our advance on Berlin. The initiative must pass back to us.

Capture Stargard, Arnswalde and the other marked positions while protecting Neuwedell. Clearing the junctions and strongpoints will support the wider Soviet offensive towards the Baltic and remove bases from which the Germans can strike south.

Do not mistake withdrawal for surrender. Enemy armour can still counterattack between the towns. Keep the infantry close to the tanks and leave a reserve where it can reach either flank.

intro:
Seelow Heights — 16 April 1945

The First Belorussian Front is to break through from the Oder and open the road to Berlin. Konev's First Ukrainian Front attacks farther south from the Neisse; Rokossovsky's Second Belorussian Front will cross the Oder later.

Your immediate objectives are Seelow, Muncheberg and the other marked positions as far as Ahrensfelde and Spreenhagen. Clear the approaches through Frankfurt and protect the staging area behind you. Berlin is the strategic destination; this battle is for the defensive belt in front of it.

The German Ninth Army holds commanding ground above the plain. Use artillery, infantry and engineers together, and bring the tanks through an opened breach. The northern flank needs protection while the neighbouring front prepares its crossing.

briliant.text:
Historical Note:

As late as April 30th and May 1st, the Nazi leaders were still playing for time, opening talks for a cease-fire in Berlin and calling on Admiral Donitz's newly proclaimed government to negotiate Germany's surrender. The Soviets held fast to the demand that Germany unconditionally surrender to all the Allies before military activities would be halted. The last ditch German attempt to sow disunity between the Allies had failed. The Soviet forces were then given the order to finish off the enemy. On May 1st 1945 at 6:30pm, the final assault on the center of Berlin began. By 3:00pm May 2nd, it was all over, and from the Reichstag waved the Hammer & Sickle. The fall of Berlin and the link up between the Soviet armies and the Allied troops led to the final collapse of Nazi Germany. The disorganized German army was no longer capable of resistance. Everywhere in Italy and Western Europe, German troops began to capitulate. On May 8th representatives of the German command signed the Act of Unconditional Surrender, thus acknowledging their total defeat...
